memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'Any children born to you after them will be yours; in the territory they inherit they will be reckoned under the names of their brothers. As I was returning from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died in the land of Canaan while we were still on the way, a little distance from Ephrath. So I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath' (that is, Bethlehem)." — Gen 48:6-7 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
In the middle of a formal legal declaration, an old man's mind wanders to a grave beside a road.

Rachel died decades ago, and Jacob still speaks of it as a fresh sorrow — "to my sorrow Rachel died." He remembers exactly where it happened, how far they were from the town, that he buried her by the roadside because there was no time to do more.

This tells us something true about grief. It does not have a deadline. Fifty years on, Jacob still carries it. He is not weak or faithless for that; he is human. If you are still grieving something everyone else has moved past, you are in good company. God has never told anyone to be finished by now.

And there is a quiet detail here that Scripture cannot resist mentioning: Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem. The place of Jacob's deepest sorrow is named as the place where, centuries later, a child would be born who came to deal with death itself.

God does not waste our places of grief. He has a habit of returning to them.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. What grief are you still carrying that others may assume you are over?
2. Have you felt pressure to "move on" faster than your heart could?
3. How does it comfort you that God works in the places of our deepest sorrow?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, You know the losses I still carry. Thank You that You do not rush my grief and that You bring life out of the very places that broke my heart. Amen.
